translations.text: "I will tell you," he said, "a dearer thing; I will say it very truly and make known a great power: now Christ is born, on this very night, the blessed child of God, in the city of David, the good Lord.
That is a joy for the race of men, a benefit to all people. There you can find him, in the city of Bethlehem, the most powerful of children.

Take this as a sign, which I can tell you with true words: that he lies there wrapped, the child in a manger, though he is king over all the earth and heaven and over the children of men, ruler of the world."

Just as he spoke that word, a countless number of angels came there to that one, a holy host from the plains of heaven, the fair people of God, and they spoke much, many words of praise to the Lord of peoples.
Then they raised a holy song, as they turned back to the plains of heaven through the clouds.
The watchmen heard how the host of angels praised almighty God very worthily with words:
"Glory be now," they said, "to the Lord himself in the highest kingdom of the heavens, and peace on earth to the children of men, to men of good will, those who acknowledge God with a pure mind."

The shepherds understood that they had been told of a mighty thing, a joyful message. They set out from there to Bethlehem, journeying by night; they had a great longing to be allowed to see Christ himself.
The angel of God had shown them everything with bright signs, so that they could go to him, to the child of God; and they soon found the Lord of the peoples, the lord of men.

Then they spoke praise to God, to the Ruler, with their words, and made known far and wide throughout the bright city what holy sign had been shown to them there from the plains of heaven, fair in the field.
The woman kept all that in her thoughts, the holy maiden, the virgin, in her mind: whatever she heard the men say.
Then the mother, out of love, nurtured him beautifully, the fairest of men, the Lord of many, the holy heavenly child.
On the eighth day men spoke together, many men, very wise men, with the maiden of God, deciding that he should have the name Saviour (Healer),
just as God's angel Gabriel, the Lord's messenger, had said it with true words and commanded the woman when she first conceived the radiant child for this world.
She had a great desire to be allowed to keep him in such a holy way; she served him very gladly.
The year moved on until the peace-child of God had reached forty days and nights.
Then they had to carry out a rite there: they had to present him at Jerusalem to the Ruler at the temple.
That was their custom then, the custom of the people of that land: no woman among the Hebrews could neglect it, if a son was born to her first; she always had to present him there at God's temple.
Then the good pair set out, Joseph and Mary both, from Bethlehem. They had the child with them, holy Christ, and went to the house of God in Jerusalem.
There they had to make his offering to the Ruler at the temple and fulfil the custom of the Jewish people.
There they found a good old man at the temple, nobly born, who had lived so many winters and summers in the light at the temple.
Often he gave praise to God there with a pure mind. He had the Holy Spirit in him, a blessed spirit. He was called Simeon.
"Now I know his age, how many winters he has: now I can bring it about that he will never grow old on this earth, here among this people."
Then Herod gave his harsh command across his kingdom: the king of the people ordered his warriors to go out,
and ordered them to cut off the heads of all those children with their own hands, all the boys around Bethlehem, as many as had been born there within two years.
The king's companions did this evil. So many little boys had to die there, free of sin.
Never before or since has there been a more terrible passing of young people, a more wretched death. Women wept, many mothers, as they saw their children destroyed:
a mother could not protect her child at all. Though she held her own child, dear and little, in her two arms, the boy still had to give up his life in front of his mother.

The killers did not shrink from crime or wickedness: with the edges of their weapons they did a great and evil deed. Many young boys fell. The mothers wept over the slaughter of their little children.
There was mourning in Bethlehem, the loudest wailing: even if someone had cut their hearts in two with a sword, no more painful thing could ever have happened in this world
to the many women, the young wives in Bethlehem: they saw their children in front of them, little boys, die in agony, bloody in their laps.
The killers punished an innocent band: the men did not hold back at all from wicked deeds. They wanted to kill the mighty one, Christ himself.
But mighty God had saved him from their hatred, so that men led him away from there by night into the land of Egypt,
men with Joseph, to the green plain, the best of lands, where a river flows, the great stream of the Nile, north to the sea, the fairest of waters.
There the peace-child of God lived as he wished, until fate carried off Herod the king, so that he left the children of men and the proud joy of men.
Then his heir was to hold power over the realm. He was called Archelaus, war-leader of helmet-bearing men: he was to rule the people of the Jews, the host around Jerusalem.
Then word came there in Egypt to the noble man [Joseph]: God's angel, the Lord's messenger, spoke there to Joseph and told him to lead the child back from there to his own land.
"Now Herod the king has given up this light," he said; "he wanted to hunt him before and put his life in danger.
Now you can lead the child in peace among your people, now that the king, that overproud man, is no longer alive."
Joseph understood God's sign completely. The good man quickly made himself ready with the maiden, since they both wanted to leave there with the child:
they carried out the bright decrees, the Ruler's will, just as he had told them before in his words.
Then Joseph and Mary, the holy household of heaven's King, went back to the land of Galilee; they lived in the town of Nazareth.
There Christ the Savior grew up among the people and became full of wisdom, and God's grace was upon him. He was dear to all his mother's kin. In his goodness that man was not like other men.
When he was twelve years old, the time came when the Jewish people were to serve their God there in Jerusalem and do his will.
Then a great crowd of Jews gathered there in the temple in Jerusalem. Mary herself was there among the company, and she had her son with her, God's own child.
When the men had performed the offering in the temple, as it was commanded in their law, carried out according to the custom of their land, then the people went back from there,

the men, as they wished; and the mighty Child of God stayed behind there in the temple, so that his mother did not truly know he was there; she thought instead that he was going on with the company, travelling with their friends.
Then afterward, on the next day, the woman of noble lineage, the blessed maiden, learned that he was not among the companions.
Then Mary's heart was full of sorrow, grieving in her heart, when she did not find the holy child among the people: the maiden of God mourned greatly.
Then they went back to Jerusalem to look for their son. They found him sitting there inside the temple, where the wise men,
very learned men, read and studied God's law, how they should give praise with their words to the one who created this world.

There in their midst sat the mighty Child of God, Christ the All-Ruler, in such a way that those who were supposed to guard the temple could not recognize him at all, and he questioned them eagerly with wise words.
They all wondered how such a childlike person could ever utter such sayings with his mouth.
There his mother found him sitting among the company, and she greeted her son, wise among the people, and spoke to him with her words:
"Why did you want to bring such sorrow on your mother, dearest of men, that I, so sad at heart, a grieving woman, had to search for you among these townspeople?"

Then the child answered her in turn with wise words: "Well," he said, "you know very well that it is fitting for me to be where I should rightfully and willingly dwell, where my mighty Father has power."
The people, the men in the temple, did not understand why he spoke that word and uttered it with his mouth:
Mary kept it all and hid it in her breast, whatever wise words she heard her child speak.
Then Joseph and Mary went back from Jerusalem. They had with them as their companion the Son of the Lord, the best of all children who were ever born, a son from a mother:
they loved him with a pure mind, and he, God's own Child, was so obedient through his humility to his kinsmen, his parents:
in his childhood he did not yet want to make his great strength known to people, that he had such might and power in this world, but he waited willingly, obedient among the people, for thirty years,
before he wanted to show any sign there, or tell his companions that he himself was the Lord of men in this middle world.
So the holy Child of God had kept to himself words and wisdom and the greatest of all understanding, a very wise mind:
no one could tell from his speech or his words that he had such understanding, that the young man had such thoughts, but he waited obediently in this way for bright signs.
The time had not yet come for him to make himself known throughout this middle world and to teach the people how they should keep their faith and do God's will.
Yet many people throughout the land knew that he had come into this light, though they could not clearly recognize him until he himself chose to tell them.

then the Ruler becomes angry with him, the mighty one, the stern of mind, and so do the children of men as well; he becomes loathsome to all the great nations, to the people, if his teachings are worthless."
So he spoke then wisely and told God's message; the guardian of the land taught his people with a pure mind. The men stood, the warriors around the Son of God, very eagerly, the men willingly:
they had a longing for the words; they pondered and were silent; they heard the Lord of the peoples tell God's law to the children of men; he promised them the kingdom of heaven and spoke to the men:
"I can also tell you, my companions, with true words, that from now on you shall be the light of this world for the children of men, fair among humankind over many a people, radiant and delightful:
your great works, by which you make your mind known, cannot be hidden, any more than the city which stands on a mountain, high on a sea-cliff,
can be hidden, the gigantic work; no more can your words, your deeds, be hidden from men in this middle-world.
Do as I teach you: let your great light shine for the people, for the children of men, so that they understand your mind,
your works and your will, and with a pure mind praise the ruling God, the heavenly Father, for it in this light, because he gave you such teachings.
No one who has a light shall hide it from people or cover it up too closely, but he shall set it up high in the hall, so that all who are inside there may see it alike, the men in the hall.
Likewise you shall not hide your holy word from the people in this land, nor conceal it from the race of men, but you shall spread it high, the command of God,
so that each and every one of the children, the people over all this land, may understand it and carry it out, as very wise men spoke it in words in former days,
when men kept the old law; and also, as I can now tell you, every one of all men shall serve God even more strongly than the old law commanded there.

Do not think in any way that I came into this world for this, that I wish to overturn the old law, to bring it down among this people, or to reject the words of the prophets, which such truthful men openly proclaimed here.
Sooner shall both pass away, heaven and earth, which now stand enclosed, than any of the words which they truly proclaimed here to these people should remain unfulfilled in this light.
I did not come into this world in order to cast down the words of the prophets, but I shall fulfil them, increase and renew them for the children of men, for the benefit of this people.
That was written long ago in the old law—you often heard men wise in words say it—:
whoever in this world does this, that he deprives another of life, robs him of life, the children of men shall sentence him to death.
Now I want to take it deeper for you, further: whoever out of enmity, one man against another, becomes angry in his mind, in his breast—because they are all brothers,
the blessed people of God, bound by kinship, men joined by family—then if anyone becomes so angry in his mind with another that he would want to rob him of life, if he could accomplish it:

You must not harshly pass any unjust judgment on any man, because the judgment comes back upon that same man, where it will be to his sorrow and become a punishment for him who here speaks wrong against others with his words.
Nor should any of you men in these dwellings, in payment or in trade, make an unjust, false measure for another man,
because it will always meet every person: just as he does to another, so it comes back against him, where he will not gladly see his sins.
I shall also tell you more about where you must guard yourselves against the greatest punishments and many evil deeds:
Why should you criticize any man, your brother, because you see a straw in his eye under his brows, and you will not remember the heavy beam that you have in your own sight, hard and heavy wood?
Let it come into your mind how you may first remove that. Then light will shine before you, and your eyes will be opened;
then afterwards you can heal the sight of the dear man, cure it in his head.

So it may be more in the mind of every man in this middle world, while he is in this world, that he himself does wrong here, than that he should concern himself with another man's offences and sins when he himself has committed more wicked deeds.

If he wants to do good, then he must first free himself from sins and release himself from evil deeds. Afterwards he can become a help to people with his teachings, once he knows himself to be pure, cleansed of sins.
You must not put your pearls before swine, or treasures of jewels, holy necklaces, because they kick them into the filth and soil them in the sand:
they do not know the difference of what is clean, of fairer ornaments. Many people here are like that, who will not listen to your holy word or follow God's teachings:
they do not know the difference of what is good, but empty words, needless things, are much dearer to them than the work and will of the God of the people.
So they are not worthy to hear your holy word, if they will not think about it in their minds, or learn it, or carry it out.
Do not tell them anything of your teachings, so that you do not waste God's speech and many messages on those people who will not believe in them, the true words.
You must also guard yourselves very cleverly among these people, as you travel through this land, so that the liars cannot deceive you with their teachings, either by words or by works.
They come to you in such clothing, fair ornaments, yet they have treacherous minds:
you can recognize them at once when you see them coming. They speak wise words, though their works are no good, the thoughts of those men.
For you know that grapes will never grow on thorns, or any wealth of fairer fruits, nor do people gather figs from briars.
You can well understand that the evil tree, where it stands on the earth, never gives good growth, nor did God create it so
that the good tree should bear anything bitter for the children of men. Instead, from every tree such growth comes into this world as is drawn to it from its root, either bright or bitter.
But this means the thoughts of the breast, the minds of many of mankind: how every man shows for himself and declares with his mouth what kind of mind he has, what thoughts lie around his heart.
He cannot hide any of this. From the evil man come malicious counsels and bitter, baleful speech, just as he holds them fastened in his breast around his heart.
His mind is always made known, and his will through his words, and his works follow accordingly.
So from the good man come wise answers, wise ones from his understanding, so that he always speaks with his words, the man with his mouth, what he has in his mind, the hoard around his heart.
From there come the holy teachings, very pleasing words, and his works shall then prosper for the people and become a delight to many thanes, just as the Ruler himself grants it to good men,

God almighty, the heavenly Lord. For without his help they cannot accomplish anything good in these dwellings, either in words or in works. Therefore the children of men shall all believe in his power alone.
I shall also show you how two ways lie here in this light, which the children of people travel, all mankind.
One of them is a wide and broad street. A great part of the host travels it, many of mankind, because men spend their minds there on worldly pleasures. It leads people to the worse side,
where they become lost, men in hell, where it is hot and black and terrible within. It is easy for the children of men to travel there, though it does them no good in the end.
Then there lies another way in this world, much narrower. Few of the host travel it, a small number of people.
The children of men do not want to walk it gladly, though it leads men to God's kingdom, into eternal life.

So take the narrow one for yourselves. Though it is not so easy for men to travel, it shall still be to the benefit of whoever goes through it. He shall receive his payment: a very lasting reward and eternal life, precious joy.
You must always ask the Lord for this and pray to the Ruler that you may take that way from the start and go on along it into God's kingdom.
He, the God of life [?], is always ready to give in return what one eagerly asks of him, what the children of men ask.
Seek your Father up in the eternal kingdom. Then you may find him afterwards to your benefit.
Make your journey known there at your Lord's doors. Then the gates of heaven will be opened and unlocked for you, so that you may go into the holy light, into God's kingdom, and see eternal life.
Before all this host I shall also tell you a true parable: whoever among all people wants to hold these teachings of mine in his heart and will think on them in his mind,
and carry them out in this land, does like a wise man who has understanding and keen thoughts. He chooses a site for his house in firm ground and builds the walls upon a rock,
where neither wind nor wave nor current of water can harm it at all. It can stand there upon the rock against all storms, because it was set so firmly on the stone.
The foundation holds it up from beneath and braces it against the wind, so that it cannot give way.
then you shall go away from those people, depart from that folk (your peace will come back to you on your own journey), and leave them in their sins
to live with their evil deeds. Seek out another city for yourselves, a great crowd of people, and do not let any of the dust follow on your feet
from the place where people will not receive you. Shake it off your shoes instead, so that it turns back on them as a shame, a witness against that people that their will is not good.
Then I tell you truly: whenever this world ends and the great day comes over mankind, the city of Sodom, which was cast down here into the abyss because of its sins by the power of fire,
brought down by fire, will then have greater peace and milder protection than those people who reject you here and will not carry out your words.
Whoever receives you with a devout heart and a gracious spirit has thereby done my will, and has also
received the ruling God, your Father, the Lord of men, the mighty Counselor, who knows all that is right.

The Ruler himself knows it, and he rewards the good will of every man for whatever good he does here, even if for the love of God he willingly gives some man a drink of water, cold water from a spring, to ease the thirst of a man in need.
These words will come true: it will never fail that he receives a reward for it, payment before God's eyes, rewards many times over, for whatever he does for love of me.

But whoever among the children of men, among the warriors, denies me before this host, I will do the same to him myself up in heaven, before the almighty Father and before all the power of his angels, before that great multitude.
And whoever of the children of men in this world will not keep silent about it, but declares before the people that he is my disciple,
him I will also acknowledge before the eyes of God, before the Father of all men, where many people will all go before the Almighty to give an account to the Mighty One.
There I will truly be a gracious protector to whoever listens to my words here and does the works that I have commanded here on this mountain."
So the Ruler's Son had truly taught the people how they should give praise to God. Then he let the crowd go from there in every direction, the host of men making their way to their homes.
They had heard the word of the King of heaven himself, his holy teaching. As long as the world lasts there will be, of words and deeds,
many among mankind across this middle-earth who are the wiser in speech, whoever has learned the sayings that the mightiest of children spoke there on the mountain.
About three nights after that, the Lord of these peoples went to the land of Galilee, where the Child of God had been invited to a feast:
a bride was to be given away there, a lovely maiden. Mary was there herself with her son, the blessed virgin, the mother of the Mighty One.
The Lord of many, God's own Child, then went with his disciples into the high house where the company, the Jews, were drinking in the guest hall.
He was at the feast with them, and there he also made it known that he had the power of God, help from the heavenly Father, the Holy Spirit, the wisdom of the Ruler.
Then it became widely known across the land of Galilee among the Jewish people how the Son of the Lord himself had turned water into wine there:
that was the first wonder of the signs that he showed there in Galilee to the Jewish people.
No one can count up or truly tell how many wonders happened afterward among the people, where the ruling Christ taught the Jewish people all day long in God's name,
promised them the kingdom of heaven and with his words warded off the torment of hell, and told them to seek God's protection, the everlasting life:

there is the light of souls, the joy of the Lord and the brightness of day, the goodness of God; there many a spirit lives in delight, whoever thinks rightly here, so that here he keeps the command of the King of heaven.
Then Christ went with his disciples away from the feast to Capernaum, he the mightiest of kings, to the famous city.
A crowd gathered, men coming to meet him, a blessed company of good people: they wanted to hear his sweet, holy words.
There a centurion came toward him, a good man, and earnestly begged the holy one for help. He said that in his household he had someone who had long been sick and lame, lying ill in his house:
"no man can heal him with his hands. Now he needs your help, my good lord."
Then the peace-child of God himself answered him right away, saying that he would come there and save the boy from that distress.
Then the man came closer to him in front of the crowd to exchange words with one so mighty:
"I am not worthy, good lord," he said, "that you should come into my house and visit my dwelling, for I am such a sinful man in words and in deeds.
I believe that you have the power to make him healthy from here, ruler, my lord:
if you speak it with your words, then at once the sickness will be undone and his body will become healthy and clean, if you give him your help.
I am an official. I have plenty of wealth, riches I have gained. Though I am under the authority of a noble king, I still have a troop of men, loyal warriors who are so obedient to me
that they leave undone no word or deed that I command them to carry out in this land; instead they go and do it and come back to their master, loyal to their lord.
Though I have wide-reaching wealth at my house and plenty of people, stout-hearted warriors, still I do not dare ask you, who are so holy,
Child of God, to come into my home and visit my dwelling, for I am so sinful; I know my misdeeds."

Then the ruling Christ, that man, spoke to his disciples. He said that nowhere among the Jews, among the descendants of Israel, had he found this man's equal, anyone in that land who had ever had more faith in God or a purer faith toward heaven:
"Now listen, as I tell you this truly in words here: many foreign peoples of mankind will yet come together from the east and from the west, God's holy people, into the kingdom of heaven:
they will be allowed to rest there in the bosoms of Abraham and of Isaac and also of Jacob, good men, and to receive both wealth and delight, and a pleasant life, good light with God.
Then many of the Jews, the sons of this kingdom, shall be bereft, deprived of such glory, and they shall lie in dark valleys in the very farthest hell.
There one may hear the men speak, where they gnash their teeth over their great anger; there is grim gnashing of teeth and greedy fire, the hard oppression of hell, heat and darkness,
black endless night as the reward for sins, for evil deeds, for whoever does not have the will to free himself before he gives up this light and departs from this world.
"Now you may go forth as you wish to your hall; there you will find the young man healthy at home:
his mind is full of joy, the child is healed, as you asked of me: it will all be done just as you hold faith firmly in your heart."
Then the official gave thanks to the King of Heaven, the all-ruling God, before the people, because he had helped him in such need.

He had then delivered his message as he wished, blessedly; he went away from there on his journey, turned as he wished to where he owned wealth, dwelling and halls: he found the child healthy, the young man.
Christ's words were then fulfilled: he had the power to show signs, so that no man over this earth can tell or reckon
what glorious deeds he performed in this middle world by his own power, what wonders he worked, for everything stood in his power, heaven and earth.
Then holy Christ went forth on his way, the Almighty, doing ⟨good⟩ every single day, the good Lord, dear to the children of men; with words he taught men God's will.
He always had many disciples as companions, the blessed people of God, a mighty force of men from many peoples, a holy host; he was good in his help, gracious to men.
Then he came with the crowd, with that splendid ⟨host⟩, the Child of God, the Savior, to the high city, to Nain: there his name was to be made famous among men.
Then the mighty Savior Christ went on until he had come near, the best of healers:
then they saw a corpse being carried there; the people were bearing a lifeless body, carrying it on a bier out through the city gate, a young man.
The mother walked behind, sorrowful in her heart, and beat herself with her hands; she lamented and mourned her child's death, the wretched woman; he was her only child:
she was a widow and had no other joy; she had placed all her joy and desire in her only son alone, until fate took him from her, the mighty decree of the Creator.
A crowd followed, a throng of townspeople, where they carried him on a bier, the young man, to the grave.
Then the Son of God showed himself there, mighty and gracious, [?] to her, and spoke to the mother; he told the widow to stop weeping and grieving for the child:
"You shall see power here, the work of the Ruler: here your wish shall be granted, comfort before this people: you need not grieve for the life of your child."
Then he went to the bier, and he himself, the Son of the Lord, touched him with holy hands, and spoke to the man; he told him, so very young, to stand up and rise from his resting place.
The man sat up, the child on the bier: the spirit came back into his breast through God's power, and he spoke in reply, the man to his kinsmen.
so that afterwards he may have the kingdom of heaven forever, through his Lord's grace, such endless wealth that no man in this world can know it.
No thegn can ever think so widely in his mind that a man's heart could hold it, so that he might truly know what good the ruling God has prepared,
all of which stands ready for any man who loves him well here and keeps his own soul for it, so that he may go into God's light."
So he taught with words. A great crowd stood around the child of God and heard him tell many parables in words about the turning of this world.
He said that a nobleman once sowed pure, clean grain in his field with his own hands. He wanted to grow a pleasant crop there for himself, fair fruit.
Then his enemy went there after him with a secret purpose, and sowed darnel over it all, the worst of weeds. Then both grew, both the grain and the weed.
Then his servants came walking to the house and told their lord, the thegns told their chieftain with bold words:
"Look, good lord, you sowed pure grain, unmixed, in your field. Now no one sees anything but more weeds growing. How could that have happened?"
Then the nobleman spoke back to the men, the lord to his thegns, and said that he could well understand it:
a hostile man, an enemy, had sown wicked weeds there after him. "He begrudged me the fruits and has ruined my crop."
Then the friends, his followers, spoke back to him and said that they wanted to go there, come with strength and pull the weeds out from there, take them out with their hands.
Then their lord answered them: "I do not want you to weed it," he said, "because you cannot guard against it,
you cannot take care as you go, even if you do not mean to, that you do not destroy too much of the grain, the shoots, and trample it under your feet.
Let them both grow on from now until the harvest time comes and the fruits in the field are ripe and ready in the field.
Then we will all go there, take it with our hands, gather the clean grain together carefully, bring it into my hall and keep it there,
so that nothing anywhere can ruin it. And we will take the weeds, bind them into bundles and throw them into the bitter fire, and let the hot flame, the insatiable fire, take them there."
Then many a man stood there, thegns keeping silent, wondering what the man of the people, the famous mighty Christ, the most powerful of children, meant, what he signified by that parable.
Then they eagerly begged the good Lord to unlock the teaching, so that the people might go on to hear the holy things.
Then their lord, the famous mighty Christ, answered them: "That is," he said, "the Son of Man:
I myself am the one who sows there. These blessed men are the pure, clean grain, who listen to me well here and do my will.
This world is the field, this broad land where the children of mankind live. Satan himself is the one who sowed such hateful teaching there after me.
He has led so many of these people, so many of the host, astray, so that they commit crimes and act according to his will.
Soon after, the man's head was brought into the hall and given there to the girl, the maiden, in front of the crowd. She carried it out to her mother.
That was the last day of the wisest of all men who ever came into this world, of all the children a woman ever bore to a man. The one exception, always, is the one whom the maiden bore,
who never knew a man in her life, except that the Ruler God from the heavenly plain mightily marked him out by the Holy Spirit. He had no equal anywhere, before or after.
The men turned to it, the men around John, his many disciples, blessed companions, and buried him in the sand, the beloved body.
They knew that he would possess God's light, precious joy together with his Lord, and would be blessed to reach the home on high.
Then the companions went away from there, John's disciples, sad at heart and holy in spirit. Their lord's death was a great sorrow to them.

Then they went to seek the Ruler's Son, mighty Christ, in the wilderness, and told him of the good man's death: how the king of the Jews had cut off the head of the most famous of men with the edges of a sword.
The Son of the Lord would say nothing harsh about it. He knew that the soul was kept holy against its enemies, in peace from its foes.
Then, when the best of teachers became known throughout the lands in the wilderness, a host gathered and people came in crowds. They had a great longing for wise words.
He, the Son of the Lord, also had the same wish: that he might invite such a band of companions into God's light and win them over gladly.
The Ruler taught many people, foreign men, all the long day, until in the evening the sun sank to its seat.
Then his twelve companions, the men, went to the Child of God and told their good lord how much hardship the people were living in there.
They said that the men in the desert land needed his help: "They cannot hold out here at all, these men, under the pressure of hunger.
Now, good lord, let them go to where they may find lodgings.
Many towns with large populations lie near here. There the men will find food to buy in the villages."
Then the Ruler Christ, Lord of peoples, spoke again. He said there was no need for this: "that through lack of food they should abandon my loving teachings.
Give these people enough; feed them here gladly." Then Philip, the wise man, had his answer ready. He said that there was such a great multitude of men there:
"Even if we had food here ready to give them, as much as we could at most pay for, if we paid out two hundred silver coins here all together,
it would still be doubtful that any of them would get even one bite. That would be so little for these people."
Then the guardian of the land, the Lord of men, spoke again and asked them eagerly what food they had obtained there as provisions.
Then Andrew answered him in front of the men and told the All-Ruler himself that they had nothing more ready in their company "except five barley loaves on our journey, and two fishes."
Then the fourth watch of the night had come — the saving Christ was watching over the seafarers —: then a great wind arose, a storm lifted up high: the waves roared, the current against the prow;
the men steered hard against the wind; their minds were troubled, their hearts full of sorrows: the seafarers did not expect to reach land themselves through the strife of the weather.
Then they saw the Ruler Christ walking on the sea itself, going on foot: he could not sink into the flood, into the sea, because his own holy power held him up.
Their minds were in fear, the men's hearts: they were afraid that a mighty fiend was doing this to deceive them.
Then their Lord spoke to them, the holy King of heaven, and told them that he was their Lord, glorious and mighty: "Now you must take hold of firm courage;
let your minds not be afraid, bear yourselves boldly: I am the Child of God, his own Son, who shall protect you against this sea, against this ocean current."
Then one of the men answered him over the side of the ship, a worthy man, Peter the good — he did not want to suffer pain, the torment of the water —:

"If you are the Ruler," he said, "good Lord, as it seems to me in my mind, then command me to go there to you over this current of the sea, dry over the deep water, if you are my Lord, protector of many."
Then mighty Christ commanded him to come towards him. He was ready at once, stepped off the prow and went forth vigorously to his Lord.

The flood held the man up through the power of God, until he began in his mind to fear the deep water, when he saw the waves driven by the wind: the waves surged around him, the high current encircled him.
Just as he doubted in his mind, the water gave way under him, and he went into the waves, sank into the sea-current,
and right after that he cried out quickly to the Son of God and earnestly begged him to save him, since he was in distress, the thane in danger.
The Lord of peoples caught him in his arms and at once asked him why he had doubted: "Why, you could well have trusted, known it as true,
that the power of the water in the sea, the sea-current, could not hinder your journey as long as you held faith in me firmly in your mind.
Now I will be a help to you, save you in this distress." Then the Almighty, the Holy One, took him by the hands:

then the clear water became firm under his feet again, and they both went together on foot until they stepped from the current over the side of the ship, and the best of all children sat down at the prow.
Then the broad water, the currents, became still, and they came to the shore, the seafarers reaching land together after the strife of the water; then they gave thanks to the Ruler,
glorified their Lord with deeds and words, fell at his feet and spoke many wise words, saying that they knew well

that he himself was truly the Son of the Lord in this world and had power over middle-earth, and that he could save the life of every man, just as he had done for them on the flood against the strife of the water.
Then the Ruler Christ, the Son of the Lord, the only Child of God, went on his way from the sea.
"I will ask all of you in words, my disciples," he said: "what do these Jewish people, this famous great nation, say about what sort of man I am?"
His friends, his disciples, answered him eagerly: "This Jewish people, these men, are not of one word.

Some say that you are Elijah, the wise prophet, who was here long ago, good among this human race; some say that you are John, the precious messenger of the Lord, who once baptized people here in water.
All of them say in words that you are one of the noble men, the prophets, who once taught these people here with words, and that you have come back into this light to guide this people."
Then the Ruler Christ spoke again: "Who do you say that I am," he said, "my disciples, my dear men?"
Then Simon Peter was not slow: he answered at once, alone before them all. He had good courage and bold thoughts, and he was loyal to his lord:
"You are the true Son of the Ruler, of the living God who created this light, Christ, the eternal King. So we all wish to say, your disciples, that you are God himself, the best of healers."
Then his Lord answered him in turn: "Blessed are you, Simon," he said, "son of Jonah. You could not have thought this up yourself or worked it out in the thoughts of your mind,
nor could any man's tongue have shown it to you in words; rather, the Ruler himself did it for you, the Father of all the children of men, so that you spoke out so profoundly about your Lord.
You shall receive a precious reward for this. You have pure faith in your Lord; your thoughts are like stone, you are as firm as the hard rock.
The children of men shall call you Saint Peter. Upon that stone my hall shall be built, God's holy house;
there his household shall gather in blessedness. The gates of hell shall not be able to hold out against your strong power.
I give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, so that after me you may have power over all Christian people. All the souls of men shall come to you.

You shall have great power: whichever of the children of men here on earth you choose to bind, to him both things are done: the kingdom of heaven is closed, and hell, the burning fire, is open to him.
Whomever you choose to unbind again, to loosen his hands, to him the kingdom of heaven is opened, the greatest of lights, and eternal life, God's green meadow.
With such things I will reward your faith. I do not want you yet to make it known to these people, this multitude, that I am the mighty Christ, God's own Son.
The Jews shall yet bind me, a guiltless man; they shall torment me terribly and inflict many torments on me in Jerusalem with spear points, seek my life with sharp blades, and deprive me of life.

Through our Lord's power I shall rise from death into this light on the third day." Then the best of thanes, Simon Peter, was very sorrowful; his mind was grieved, and the warrior spoke privately to his Lord:
"The good Ruler of the kingdom," he said, "shall not will that you should ever suffer such great torment among this people. There is no need for that at all, holy Lord."
Then his Lord, the famous, mighty Christ, answered him in turn, for he was kindly disposed toward him in his heart: "What! Now you are opposed to my will," he said, "best of thanes!
Then they heard the great crowd passing, and at once the two stone-blind men asked eagerly which powerful man among the people was the foremost there, the highest in rank.
Then a man answered them and said that Jesus Christ from Galilee, the best of healers, the highest, was travelling there with his people.
Then the hearts of both blind men grew glad, when they knew that the Child of God was among the crowd.
Then they called out to him, loudly to the holy Christ, and begged him to give them help: "Lord, Son of David,
be merciful to us by what you do. Save us from this distress, as you do for so many of humankind. You are good to many; you help and you heal."
Then the people began to hold them back with words, telling them not to shout so loudly to Christ the Ruler.
They would not obey them in this, but kept shouting loudly, more and more, over the crowd of people.

The Healer, the best of all children, stood still and ordered them to be brought to him, led through the people. Before the crowd he spoke to them wisely and gently: "What help from me do you two want to have here?" he said.
They asked the Holy One to open their eyes and grant them this light, so that they might see the joy of people, the bright shining of the sun, the beautiful world.

The Ruler did it. He touched them with his hands and gave his help to it, so that the eyes of both blind men were opened, and through the power of God they could make out earth and heaven, light and people.
Then they gave praise to God and glorified our Lord because they could enjoy the light of day. Both of them went with him and followed him on his journey.
The benefit was granted to them, and the Ruler's work was also made known far and wide and proclaimed to many.
A very powerful symbol was shown there, where the blind men sat by the road, suffering torment, deprived of light.

Yet it stands for the children of men, all humankind: how mighty God, in the beginning, by his power alone, himself made the two spouses, Adam and Eve, and gave them the way upward, the kingdom of heaven.
But then the hateful one came too near them, the fiend with his malice and wicked deeds. He deceived them with sins, so that they lost eternal beauty, the light.
They were cast into a more hateful place. Human beings were thrown out into this middle world. Here they suffered slavery in darkness, endured the paths of exile, and went without wealth.
They forgot God's kingdom and served enemies, the children of fiends. In return, those enemies paid them wages of fire in hot hell.

Therefore the children of men were blind in their minds in this middle world, because they did not recognize him, the mighty God, the heavenly Lord, who had created them with his hands and made them according to his will.
This world was then so far turned aside, forced down into darkness, into slavery, into the valley of death.
They sat then by the Lord's road, sorrowful in mind, waiting for God's help. It could not come to them until the ruling God, the mighty Lord, chose to send into this middle world
his own Son, so that he might unlock the light for the children of men and open eternal life to them, so that they could truly know the All-Ruler, the mighty God.
I can also tell you, if you will turn your minds to it and listen, so that you may recognize the power of the Savior: how his coming became a help to many in this middle-world,
yes, what the Lord himself meant by many of his deeds, and why the famous city that stands there in the land of the Jews, built with walls, is called Jericho:
it is named after the moon, after the bright heavenly light. The moon cannot escape its times; every single day it does one or the other: it wanes or it waxes.
So do the children of men here in this world, in this middle-world: they go and follow one another; the old die, and young ones come again after them, grown men, until fate takes them away in turn.
That is what the child of God, the good one, meant when he went out of the city, out of Jericho: that the blindness could not be healed for the children of men before then,
so that they might see the bright light, the eternal beauty, until he himself here in this middle-world took on humanity, flesh and body.
Then the children of men in this world became aware of it, those who had sat here before in torment, in sins, without sight, suffering in darkness
— they perceived that a Savior had come to this people as a help from the kingdom of heaven, Christ, the best of all kings; they could recognize him at once and sense his coming.
Then the men cried out a great deal to the mighty God, that the Ruler would afterwards be merciful to them.
But the heavy sins which they themselves had committed before held them back strongly and hindered them from that faith.
Yet the sins could not keep the people from their desire; instead they cried loudly to the ruling God until he granted them their healing, so that they might see eternal life,

the open, everlasting light, and go into the bright dwellings. That is what the blind men signified who cried loudly there by the city of Jericho to the child of God, asking him to grant them their healing, light in this life:
though the people travelling on the road in front and behind tried hard to stop them with words. That is what wicked sins do to mankind in this middle-world.
Hear now how the blind men acted after they had been healed, so that they could see the light of the sun:
they went off together with their Lord, followed his journey, and spoke many words in praise of the shepherd of the land.
So the children of men still do far and wide throughout this world, since the ruling Christ enlightened them with his teachings and granted to good men eternal life,
God's kingdom, the high light of heaven, and his help besides, to whoever acts so that he may follow his way.

Then Christ the Savior, the good one, drew near to Jerusalem. Many people came out there to meet him, gladly and with good will. They received him warmly and strewed the road before him with their garments and also with plants,
with bright blossoms and with branches of trees, and the field with lovely palms, all as befitted his journey, since the Son of God meant to go to the famous city.
A great crowd of people thronged around him in joy, and the multitude gladly raised a song of praise. They gave thanks to the Ruler that the son of David himself had come there to visit the people.
So then he, the mighty Lord, cleared and set in order the holy house, and he was a help to many of mankind, those who had heard of his great power from afar and came travelling there over a long way.
Many a sick person was there; the lame were healed and the crippled likewise, and the blind were cured.
So the Child of God did this, willingly, for the people, because everything concerning the life of these people, and also this land likewise, stands in his power.
Then the ruling Christ, the dear guardian of the land, stood before the sanctuary and observed the minds of the people and their intentions:
he saw a great crowd bringing treasures into the famous house, giving gold and fine woven cloth, precious ornaments. Christ the Lord watched all that wisely.
Then a widow also came there, a poor woman, and went to the temple, and she laid two brass coins in the treasure-house. Her heart was single-minded, full of good will.
Then the ruling Christ, the man, spoke to his disciples and said that she had brought a much greater gift there than any other son of man:
"If wealthy men have brought possessions here," he said, "many treasure-hoards, they have kept more of their gathered wealth for themselves at home.
This widow did not do so. She gave to this temple all the wealth she had gathered, so that she left herself no goods at all in her dwelling.
Therefore her gifts are greater and more worthy to the Ruler, because she gave them to this house of God with such good will.
For this she shall receive payment, a very lasting reward, because she has such faith."
So I have heard that there in the temple the ruling Christ, the Lord of men, taught with words every single day.
A crowd stood around him, a great people of the Jews, and they heard him speak his good words sweetly.
One man among the crowd became so blessed that he began to store it up in his mind; they learned the teachings that the guardian of the land, the Child of the Lord, spoke, all in parables.
To others, in turn, Christ's teachings, the words of the Ruler, were very hateful: their minds were hostile, all those who were highest in the host, the foremost among the people:

in their hostility they intended to set traps with their words. To help them they had brought in adversaries, men of the highest man [probably Herod], Herod's retainer, who stood present there with hostile intent,
so that he might overhear their words, and so that, if they caught him, those people might then lay fetters and limb-bonds on him, the sinless one.
Then the companions went up to him with bitter minds, so that they, hostile adversaries, spoke these words to the Child of God:
"Well, you are a prophet to all peoples," they said, "you teach so much truth: you need not avoid any man in the least because of his power,
but you always speak what is right and with your teachings lead the companies of men onto God's way. No one among this people can find fault in you. Now we must ask you,
mighty king, what right the emperor of Rome has, who seeks tribute here from this people and has reckoned what we must pay him every year as head-tax.
Tell us what you think about this in your mind: is it right or is it not? Counsel your countrymen well: we have need of your teachings."
They wanted him to speak against it, but he could clearly see their hostile intent. "Why, you liars," he said, "do you test me so boldly?
It will do you no good that you hypocrites now secretly want to trap me." Then he ordered them to bring out the coins for him to look at, "the ones you are required to give in that tax."
The Jews brought out a silver coin, and many looked at how it was minted. In the middle shone the emperor's image, their lord's head, which they could clearly recognize.
Then the holy Christ asked them whose likeness had been put on it.
They said it was the likeness of the world-emperor of Rome, "who has power over all this kingdom in this world."
"Then I will truly tell you myself, here," he said, "that you should give him what is his, give the lord of the world what he has a right to, and give the ruling God what is his:
that is, your souls, the spirits of men." Then the Jews lost heart in that assembly.
Those wicked men could not use words to trap him as they wanted to, because God's child of peace guarded himself against the hostile men and spoke the truth back to them.
He told them true words, though they were not blessed enough to take them in the way that would have been good for them.
Yet they would not let it go. Instead they had a woman brought out in front of the crowd who had committed a crime, a plain wrong.
The woman had been caught in adultery. She was liable to lose her life, so that the children of men would take her life and deprive her of it, as was written in their law.

Then the bold people began to question him, hostile in their words. They asked what they should do to the woman: whether they should kill her or let her live, or what judgment he would give about such deeds.
"You know," they said, "how Moses commanded this people in true words that every woman who forfeits her life through adultery should then be struck down by men's hands with hard stones.
Now you can see her standing here, caught in sin. Say what you want done about it."

The adversaries wanted to trap him with words. If he said that they should let her live and spare her life, then the Jewish people would say that he was speaking against the law of their ancestors, the law of the land of the people.
But if he ordered them to take the young woman's life in front of the crowd, then they would say that he did not carry in his breast the kind of merciful mind that the child of God should have.
So either way they wanted to blame holy Christ for his words, whichever answer he gave there before the crowd as his judgment.
But the Lord Christ knew those men's thoughts and their hostile intent very well. Then he spoke to the crowd, to all those men:
"Whichever of you is without cruel sins," he said, "let that man go up to her himself and be the first to throw a stone at her with his hand."
So the Jews stood there, thinking, and kept silent. No man could find any [?] answer against what he had said. Every man remembered his own wicked thoughts, his own sins.
Then their fame lives on after them, a good word among men." So the disciples of Christ, nobly born men, became of one mind, willing to do their lord's will.
Then holy Christ himself told his companions that Lazarus had fallen asleep from his sickness: "He has given up this light; he has been put to sleep in his dwelling.
Now let us go on that journey and wake him, so that he may see this world again, the light, living. Then your faith will afterwards be made firmer still."

Then he went away from there over the river, the good Son of God, until he came with his disciples to Bethany, the Child of the Lord himself with his companions, where the two sisters, Mary and Martha, sat sorrowful in grief of heart.
Many of the Jewish people from Jerusalem had gathered there, who wanted to comfort the women with words, so that they would not grieve so much over the young man's death, the loss of Lazarus.
As the Guardian of the land then went toward the dwellings, the coming of God's Child was made known there, that he, so mighty, was outside the town.
Then both of the women had a strong desire for this, when they knew that the Ruler, the peace-child of God, was journeying toward them.
Then the greatest of joys for the women was the coming of the Lord and the hearing of Christ's words.
Weeping, Martha went, sorrowful, to exchange words with the Mighty One, and she spoke to the Ruler, troubled in her mind:
"If you, my lord," she said, "best of saviours, had been nearer, good Healer, then I would not now have to suffer such harm,
bitter heart-sorrow; then my brother Lazarus would not now be dead, gone from this light, but could go on living at home, full of life.
Yet I, my lord, believe clearly in you, best of teachers, that whatever you wish to ask of the bright Lord, he will grant it to you at once, God almighty, and fulfil your wish."
Then the Ruler Christ spoke an answer back to the woman: "Do not let your spirit grow dark within you over this," he said.
"I can tell you with true words that there is no doubt of this: your brother shall rise from death in his body, through God's command, through the Lord's power."
"I [?] believe so," she said, "that it shall happen so, whenever this world ends and the glorious day passes over mankind,
that he will then rise up from the earth on the Day of Judgment; then every one of mankind will come alive from death through God's might and arise from rest."
Then the powerful Christ almighty told the woman in plain words that he himself was the Son of the Lord, both life and light for the children of men, for them to rise again:
"Whoever here believes in me shall never die or lose life.
Though the children of men cover him with earth and bury him deep, he is no more dead for that: the flesh is buried, the life is kept, his soul is safe."
Then the woman at once spoke back to him with her words: "I believe that you are the true one," she said, "Christ, the Son of God.
One can recognize that well, and know it from your words, that you have power over heaven and earth through the holy decrees."
Then, as I have heard, the other of the women came walking there, Mary, sorrowful; many of the Jewish people went after her.
"The Father of all the children of men has himself blessed you. You may enjoy these good things and rule this wide kingdom, because you often did my will,
followed me gladly and were generous to me with your gifts when I was gripped by thirst and hunger, caught by frost, or lay in fetters, shut up in prison.
Help often came to me there from your hands. You were kind to me in your hearts and visited me with honour."
Then that host speaks back to him: "My good Lord," they say, "when were you ever caught like that and gripped by such needs as you tell of before this people? What do you mean, mighty one?
When did any man see you gripped by such needs? Why, you have power over all peoples, and likewise over the treasures that the children of men have ever won in this world."
Then the ruling God speaks to them in turn: "Whatever you did," he says, "in the name of your Lord,
whatever good you gave, for God's honour, to the people who are the least here, among those who now stand in this multitude and were poor men out of humility,
because they did my will — whatever of your wealth you gave them and did for them out of love, your Lord himself received it. That help came to the King of heaven.
Therefore the holy Lord will reward your faith: he gives you eternal life."
Then the Ruler, the Lord, turns to his left hand, to the wicked men, and tells them that they must pay for what they did, those men, for their wicked works: "Now you must go away from me," he says,

"go, accursed as you are, into the eternal fire that was prepared there for God's enemies, the host of fiends, because of their wicked works. For you did not help me when hunger and thirst tormented me terribly, or when I went without clothing, wretched in spirit.
I was in great need, and I had no help there when I was bound, locked in fetters on my limbs, or when a sickbed held me in grievous illness.
Then you would not visit me there at all in my sickness. Nothing was worth enough to you to make you think of me. Therefore you must suffer in hell, in darkness."
Then that people speaks back to him: "O ruling God," they say, "why will you speak like this against this host, and address this multitude so?
When were you ever in need of men, of any good from people? Why, they had all of it by your gifts, the wealth in this world." Then the ruling God speaks again:
"When you, warriors, despised in your hearts the poorest of the children of men, the least of men,
held them hateful in your minds and denied them your kindness, then you did the same to your Lord and refused him your wealth.
Therefore the ruling God, your Father, will not receive you. Instead you must go into the fire, into deep death, and serve the devils, the angry enemies, because you acted this way before."
Then, after those words, the host splits in two, the good and the evil.
The damned men go into hot hell, sorrowful at heart. The men ruined by their own deeds receive torment, evil without end.
Then the King of heaven leads the pure peoples up from there into the lasting light. There is eternal life there, God's kingdom, made ready for good people.
that it shall nevertheless turn to harm for him, become a punishment; when he sees his fate and looks upon the end of [?] his toil, then he knows it to be true
that it would have been a better thing for him, much better, if he had never been born alive into this light, than that he should receive that reward, evil toil, for his wicked counsel."
Then each of the men began to look at the other, looking about in sorrow; their minds were sore, grieving about their hearts: they heard their lord speak words of grief.
The men worried about which of the twelve he meant by this, the guilty wrongdoer who had bargained there with the people for the treasure.
It was not easy for any of the thegns to confess such malice, such wicked thoughts. Each of the men denied it. They all became afraid,
and they did not dare to ask, until a worthy man, Simon Peter, made a sign (he did not dare to say it himself) to John the good:

he was the dearest of the thegns to the Child of God in those days, the greatest in His love, and he was allowed to rest there on the lap of the mighty Christ, and he lay on His breast and leaned his head there:
there he received many holy secrets and deep thoughts. Then he spoke to his Lord and began to ask Him:
"Who shall that be, my lord," he said, "who means to sell you, most powerful of kings, to the people of your enemies?
We would greatly like to know this, Ruler." Then Christ the Healer had His answer ready: "See the one to whom I give some of my food here into his hand before these men:
he has wicked thoughts and bears a bitter mind; he shall hand me over into the power of killers, to enemies, where they will seek my life and my being."

After that He took some of the food before the men and gave it to the wicked wrongdoer, into Judas's hand. He Himself spoke to him in front of His companions and told him to go quickly away from His people:
"Do as you intend," He said, "do what you must do: you cannot hide your will any longer. Fate is at hand; the time has now drawn near."
As soon as the faithless one received the food and tasted it with his mouth, the power of God left him, and fiends went into his body,
hateful creatures. Satan pressed painfully upon him, hard about his heart, since the help of God had abandoned him in this light.
So it is woe to the people who must change lords in this way under this heaven.
Then Judas went out from there, eager for malice: the thegn had a grim mind against his lord. By then it was dark night, very gloomy.
The Son of the Lord continued there at the meal with His disciples. There the Ruler consecrated both wine and bread, the King of Heaven made them holy,
broke it with His hands and gave it out among His disciples. He thanked God and gave thanks to Him who created all things, the world and its joys, and He spoke many words:
"Believe this clearly," He said, "that this is my body and likewise my blood: I give you both of them here together to eat and to drink.
This I shall give and pour out on earth, and with my body I shall redeem you for God's kingdom, into eternal life, into the light of heaven.
Always remember to carry out what I do at this meal; proclaim this before the multitude:
He shall comfort you afterwards and become a help to you. He will remind you of the teachings that I have taught you in many words.
He will give you understanding in your breast, delightful teaching, so that from now on you carry out the words and the works that I commanded you in this world."
Then the mighty one, the saving Christ, rose up inside the hall and went away from there by night with his companions. Christ's disciples went sorrowfully, deeply mourning, sad at heart.
Then he went up onto the high Mount of Olives. He was used to going up there with his disciples. Judas, the evil-minded man, knew that well, because he had often been on the mountain with him.
There the Son of God spoke to his disciples: "You are so troubled now," he said, "now that you know of my death.
Now you mourn and weep, and these Jews are delighted. This crowd rejoices, they are glad in their hearts, this world is full of joy.

Yet that will very soon be reversed. Then their minds will be sore, then they will mourn in their hearts, and afterwards you shall rejoice for ever, for no reversal of your blissful life will ever come.
Therefore you need not grieve over these events or lament my departure, for from it help shall come to the children of men."
Then he told his disciples to wait there on the mountain, and said that he wished to climb higher among the rocky cliffs to pray.
Then he told three thanes to go with him: James and John and the good Peter, the bold-hearted thane. They went gladly together with their lord.

Then on the mountain the Son of God told them to bow down in prayer. He told them to call on God and pray earnestly that he would ward off from them the power of the tempters, the will of the hostile ones, so that the adversary,
the wicked destroyer, could not make their minds doubt. And then the Son of the Lord himself, the mighty one, the most powerful of kings, bowed down on his knees, forward to the earth.
He called on the good Father of all peoples and spoke sorrowfully in words of grief. His mind was troubled; his spirit was shaken because of his human nature; his flesh was afraid.
Tears fell from him, and his precious sweat dripped down just as blood comes welling from wounds. Then there was a struggle within the child of God between the spirit and the body.

The one, the spirit, was eager to set out on the way forth into God's kingdom. The other, Christ's body, stood in anguish: it did not want to give up this light, but was troubled in the face of death.
He kept calling out to the Lord, more and more as time went on. He called on the mighty one, the high Father in heaven, holy God, the Ruler, with his words:
"If mankind cannot now be saved," he said, "unless I give my dear body for the children of men to be tormented terribly,
then, if that is your will, I am willing to endure it. I take the cup in my hand and drink it in your honour, my Lord and master, mighty protector.
Do not look here to the comfort of my flesh. I shall fulfil your will: you have power over all."

Then he went back to where he had earlier left his disciples to wait on the mountain. The child of God found them sleeping in their sorrow. Their minds were sore because they would have to part from their lord.
In the same way, it is a heartache to any man when he has to leave a beloved lord and give up one so good.
"When the sun was shining, the precious light of day, you would not do me any harm in that light,
and now your people lead me off into the dark night, just as one does with a thief, when one wants to seize him and he has forfeited his life, a criminal."

Then the band of the Jews, a grim people, a crowd of haters, seized the Son of God. They swarmed around him, the arrogant mob of men (they paid no heed to the wickedness), and bound his hands together with harsh bonds, his arms with fetters.
He had no need to endure such cruel torment and hardship, or to suffer such punishment, but he did it for the sake of these people, because he wanted to redeem the children of men,
to fetch them from hell into the kingdom of heaven, into its wide riches. Therefore he said nothing against what they wanted to inflict on him out of malice.
Then the proud people of the Jews grew so arrogant, and the crowd so boastful, at being able to lead the holy Christ in bonds on his limbs and to bring him along in fetters.
The enemies went back from the mountain to the town. The child of God walked among the armed band with his hands bound, sorrowing, down to the valley.
His dear companions had now deserted him, just as he himself had told them before.
Yet it was not out of any cowardice that they abandoned the beloved child of God. It had been the word of the prophets long before that it would happen so, and therefore they could not avoid it.
Then John and Peter, the two men, went after the crowd, following at a distance. They were very eager to know what the grim Jews wanted to do to the child of God, their Lord.
Then they came down from the mountain to the town, where their bishop was, the guardian of their temple, and there the proud men led him, the warriors, within the enclosure.
There was a large fire there, a fire in the courtyard, set in the middle of the people, made in front of the crowd. The Jews went there to warm themselves, and left the Son of God waiting in bonds.
There was a great noise there, the din of exultant men. John was already known to the high priest, and so he was able to push his way into the court with the people.
Peter, the best of all thanes, stood outside there. The gatekeeper would not let him follow his Lord until his friend John asked one of the Jews to let him go on into the courtyard.
There a deceitful woman came walking toward him. She belonged to one of the Jews, a servant of their lord, and then the unlovely maid spoke to the thane:
"Why, you could be one of the men," she said, "a disciple from Galilee, of the one who stands over there with his arms bound."
Then Simon Peter at once grew afraid, faint in his heart. He said that he did not understand the woman's words and that he was not that lord's thane.
Then he denied it in front of the crowd and said that he did not know the man. "I don't know what you are talking about," he said. The power of God, the steadfastness, had left his heart.
Wandering, he went on among the people until he came to the fire, and went to warm himself.
There a woman also began to throw wicked words at him: "Here you can see your enemy," she said. "This is certainly a disciple of Christ, his own companion.
"Now you need not wait any longer," he said, "for this crowd's testimony, now that such words come from him, blasphemy from his mouth.

Many men here have now heard it, warriors in this hall: he makes himself out to be so mighty that he claims he is God. What sentence do you Jews want to pass on this? Do such words now make him worthy of death?"
The whole crowd, the people of the Jews, spoke out: he had forfeited his life and so deserved punishment.
Yet nothing he had done justified what the Jewish people there in Jerusalem did when they condemned the Lord's Son, who was without sin, to death.
Then the Jewish people were eager and proud of their deeds, of whatever harm they could do to the child of God now that he was a prisoner.

Then they surrounded him with their crowd and struck him on his cheeks, on his face, with their hands. All this was done to him in mockery. The crowd of enemies heaped wicked words on him, words of scorn.
The child of God stood firm among his enemies. His arms were bound. He patiently endured whatever bitterness the people brought him. He was not angry at all at the crowd's hostility.
Then angry men took the child of God, bound as he was, and led him to the place where the people's assembly house was.
There many thanes thronged around their commander. Their lord's representative from Rome was there, sent by the one who then ruled the empire.
He had come from the emperor. He had been sent among the Jewish people to govern the land and was the ruling counsellor there.
He was called Pilate. By birth he came from the land of Pontus. He had a great force with him, people gathered in the assembly house, a throng of men.

Then faithless men, the Jewish people, handed over the Son of God into the hands of hostile people. They said he had forfeited his life and should be punished with the edges of weapons, with sharp blows.
The crowd of Jews would not push into the assembly house. The people stood outside and spoke from there to the crowd inside.

They would not go into the gathering among foreigners, so that they would not hear unjust words there or anything wicked being judged on that day. They said they wanted to keep the holy time, their Passover, in complete purity.
Pilate received the Ruler's child, who was without sin, from the wicked men.
Then Judas's mind became full of sorrow when he saw his Lord handed over to death. After that the deed began to grieve him in his heart, that he had sold his sinless Lord.

So he took the silver in his hand, the thirty coins he had been given for his Lord. He went to the Jews and told them about his terrible deed, his sins, and eagerly offered to give the silver back to them:
"I have bought it so horribly with my Lord's blood," he said, "that I know it will bring me no good."
The Jewish people would not accept it. Instead they told him to consider such sins himself, what he had done against his lord:
"You saw to that yourself," they said. "Why do you come to us about it now?
Don't blame this crowd for it!" Then Judas went away from there to God's temple in deep sorrow and threw the silver into the temple. He did not dare keep it any longer.
Then soon after that it came to pass, to the women's joy, that they heard such words spoken, the power of God made known. They were still so shaken then, and so frightened [?]:
they went away from there, from the grave, and told Christ's disciples of the wondrous sight, where they were waiting in sorrow for such a comfort.
Then the guards of the Jews also came into the city, who had sat over the grave all the long night and guarded the body there, the corpse.
They told the host of the Jews what terrors had come upon them there, a wondrous sight. They told it in words, all as it had been done by the Lord's power; they did not hide it in their minds.
Then the Jewish people offered them many treasures, gold and silver, and gave them much wealth, so that they would not tell it further or make it known to the multitude:
"But say that your weary minds lulled you to sleep, and that his companions came there and stole him from the stone.
Always hold to that in dispute, and hold to it eagerly. If it becomes known to the governor, we will help you against that highest lord, so that he does you no harm and nothing hateful."

Then they took many precious treasures from the people and did all as they had begun (they did not govern their own will). They made it widely known to the people throughout the land, for they wanted to raise such lies about the holy Lord.
But the minds of Christ's disciples were healed again when they heard the good women proclaim the might of God;
then they were glad in their hearts. Both of them went to the grave: John and Peter ran quickly.
The good John arrived first and stood over the grave, until Simon Peter came soon afterwards, a man renowned for courage, and he went into the grave.
There he saw the shroud of God's child, the linen grave-clothes of his lord, lying there, in which the body had been beautifully wrapped before;
the cloth lay apart, the one that had covered the head of holy Christ, the mighty Lord, while he was in this resting place.

Then John also went into the grave to see the wondrous thing. Soon after that his faith was unlocked, so that he knew that his Lord was to come back into this light in glory, rising up from death, up from the earth.
Then John and Peter went away again from there, and Christ's disciples, his companions, came together.
Then one of the women stood sad-hearted for a second time, weeping over the grave; her mind was full of grief. That was Mary Magdalene.
The thoughts of her heart, her very mind, were mixed with sorrows. She did not know where she should seek the Lord on whom her help depended.
She could not stop her lamenting then; the woman could not leave off weeping. She did not know where she should turn; her thoughts were confused.
Then she saw the mighty Christ standing there, though she could not clearly recognize him until he wished to make himself known and say that it was he himself.
He asked why she was weeping so sorely, so grievously, with hot tears. She said that she did not know for certain about her lord, what had become of him:
